text: A half crown is not much money, which is exactly why it is the sum named. An earl puts his son out of the house and sets the smallest possible price on his return: earn the coin, and prove yourself worthy of confidence. Giles Bateson has just been expelled from college for misconduct, so the condition is not about money at all but about the fact that he has never earned anything. Maurice Tourneur made the film in the United States in 1914, and the England on screen is assembled out of hedges, cottages and titles - idyll is in the title and it governs the treatment, keeping the disgrace light enough to be mended. Sixty minutes, one errand, a young man of rank discovering that work exists. The pleasure is in how much a plot of 1914 will hang from a single small coin.

A Confederate spy, two sisters, a group of Native Americans and a firing squad, all arranged so that a comedian can keep moving. Jack's assignment is a shipment of gold he is meant to intercept for the South, and every obstruction in his way is built to be escaped rather than survived. That is the shape of much mid-1920s screen comedy: a premise loose enough to admit any interruption, with the timing carried by whatever fits inside the frame. What makes this one odd is the setting. Clarence G. Badger takes the Civil War, the American subject most reliably handled with reverence, and treats it as flat ground for improvisation. Seventy minutes. The war supplies uniforms, distances and a reason for everybody to be armed; nothing else is asked of it.

Every gallon that reaches Los Angeles left a place that is drier for having supplied it. Fifty-seven minutes is a strange length for a subject that size, too long for a segment and too short for the history, and Pat O'Neill's film is not built as history anyway. It is offered as a reflection, which here means holding the city and the emptied country around it inside the same stretch of time, so the two can be looked at rather than explained. Sundance gave it the grand jury prize for documentary in 1989. What the film wants is patience with landscape: the sprinkler and the desert are one event seen from opposite ends of a pipe, and the camera will wait for the resemblance to become visible. Nature and man, in the old phrasing, are a single circuit.

Drink, jazz and abortion share a carriage, and the carriage is going to one place. Fifty-one minutes, 1930: sinners board a train whose destination the title has already given away, and each vice is laid out with the directness of a sermon that expects everybody in the room to keep up. James Gist is not staging drama so much as preaching with a camera. Sin is catalogued rather than dramatised, and the fantasy device of a train - a schedule, a route, a terminus - exists so a moral list can be arranged as a journey, which is the oldest way of making a warning legible. What survives is a very specific American anger at 1930 itself: at the music, at the drinking, at what women decide, delivered as prophecy and shot as though prophecy were an event a camera could attend.

Steel-driving is repetitive labour, and repetition is what animation is made from: one small movement, fixed, photographed, done again. George Pal has seven minutes. John Henry arrives already grown and already the strongest hammer man on the line, and then a new steel-driving machine turns up that does not tire, does not eat and has no livelihood to lose. The legend supplies the cadence and the film keeps to it, so the telling moves by rhythm rather than talk. Seven minutes is the length of a bus ride, and the Academy gave it the award for animated short. The better joke is on the method: every blow on screen had to be staged by hand, one frame at a time, which puts the animator on the far end of the same hammer.

The word arrives before the soldiers do: call the islanders communists, and the army has a reason to be sent. Everything that follows comes from a label fixed on people whose complaint was against their own police. O Muel takes a hundred and eight minutes over it, which for this kind of history is a long time to stay away from battle; the weight falls instead on villagers deciding what to do about houses, food, animals and each other while an armed force moves in their direction. History in the register of chores. The film took the World Cinema Dramatic grand jury prize at Sundance, one measure of how far a story told at that scale can travel. A village and a word are enough; the premise needs no enlarging.

An assembly line worker decided that the man in front of him was the reason his job was disappearing, and he was wrong twice: about the cause, and about who the man was. Vincent Chin was an automotive engineer, taken for Japanese at a moment when Japanese cars were the standing explanation for what had happened to American ones. Christine Choy spends eighty-seven minutes on the killing and then on the machinery that handled it, moving from the street into the courts, where the argument shifts from what occurred to what it ought to cost. Two acts of blaming sit inside one case, and the film never draws the line between them out loud. It was restored by the Academy Film Archive and The Film Foundation with the Museum of Chinese in America, which is a way of saying the case did not close when the paperwork did.

A cub reporter, thrilled with his first murder, writes that the suspect is a woman named Jane, and it is in print before anyone has checked. That error is the engine. Clem spends the rest of the film undoing his own copy in the company of the person it damaged, which turns an investigation into restitution rather than curiosity. Sixty-two minutes, 1928, silent, and the tempo belongs to a newsroom: things happen because an edition is closing, not because anyone has reasoned them out. Frank Capra's name is the reason the film gets pulled off the shelf now, but the plainness is what holds - a byline is power over a stranger's name, and a young man who wants one badly will spend somebody to get it. The plot never argues that. It proceeds as if it were obvious.

Warfare with a season, a form and agreed rules for stopping: that is what Robert Gardner went to New Guinea to film. The Dani of the Baliem Valley are followed through a cycle in which fighting sits inside ordinary life instead of interrupting it, and eighty-four minutes is long enough for the pattern to come round more than once. The film is also a document of 1964, when ethnographic cinema still assumed that one people could be explained to another at length, in English, from outside. Both things are on the screen at the same time, and the second does not cancel the first. The camera is patient with work, with distance, with how long it takes to walk somewhere. Because the subject is a cycle and not a story, the shape has to be found in recurrence, which is harder than plot.

A pilot comes home from the war decorated and goes back to his old job: railroad detective. The title promises aviation and the assignment delivers accounting - twenty-five thousand dollars of payroll gone in a satchel, an employee missing, a gang somewhere along the line. In 1926 the combination held together, since flying was still a credential rather than a career, and a company that shipped money by rail needed men who could follow it. Sixty-five minutes gives Richard E. Norman three problems and a fixed clock, which is a useful discipline: character emerges from the order in which the tasks get solved. The war stays in the background and is never a wound. What is left is heroism converted into employment, and a hero asked to earn it again on a payroll case.

Be like Dad, Keep Mum: the wartime slogans are painted on the walls inside the film, and the film behaves like one of them, stretched to a hundred and two minutes. Careless talk is both subject and mechanism, which lets Thorold Dickinson build a thriller where the danger is not a spy's cleverness but a sentence passed on in good faith by someone with no idea what it contains. Instruction usually flattens drama; here it concentrates it, because the audience of 1943 was being asked the same thing as the characters and sat in the cinema as their neighbours. The National Board of Review put it among the ten best of the year, an unusual result for a picture with a lesson to deliver. The mystery is not who did it. It is how far a sentence gets, and through whose mouth.

A new widescreen process was introduced to the world with a sailing ship. Windjammer follows the full-rigged Christian Radich out of Oslo with a complement of trainees aboard, across the Atlantic, down through the Caribbean, up to New York and home again: two hours and twenty minutes of voyage that doubles as a demonstration of what CINEMIRACLE could do with horizon and height. The two purposes agree with each other. Rigging goes up, screens went wide, and a boy climbing toward a yardarm is worth more to a projection system than anything a studio could stage. It is a travel record with a commercial errand attached, and the National Board of Review still counted it among the year's ten best. What holds up is the work: a training cruise means jobs assigned daily, and the camera has time to watch them done.

Three men, a projector, and the distances between Australian towns. The father runs the show, the son carries things, and the piano player supplies everything the silent films lack; the route itself is the business. A 1977 film about early cinema could easily have been homage, and this one is more taken with the freight - that showing pictures for money meant hauling equipment across a continent and setting it up again in a room never built for it. The comedy is that of a small enterprise with large overheads. AACTA prizes went to three of its performances, which suits a picture running on the friction between a man who intends to be an impresario and the two people who must go wherever he goes.

Squatters on a rich man's land, and a girl who takes up their case. Eighty minutes was a substantial commitment in 1914, and Edwin S. Porter spends it on a property fight: who may stay, who decides, and what a claim without paper is worth. The film keeps the argument on the ground where it happens, among people whose homes exist at somebody else's discretion, and it lets the young woman do the arguing, which puts a girl against an owner and a deed. Melodrama of the period liked its poor virtuous and its rich capable of reform, and the picture works inside that arrangement rather than against it. What holds now is the concreteness of the threat. Eviction is not a theme in this story; it is a thing that can happen on a particular morning.
